883.title: Chardi kala in the century
883.hook: a people hunted for decades sang at night
883.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila before sleep, and the Ardas closes with a wish for chardi kala through the Name and the good of all; Sikhs greet hardship with the phrase chardi kala as an ideal of spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sites of the two ghallugharas, gurdwaras now standing in the fields. The places remember. Today, two words near the end of the Ardas.

Two words sit near the very end of the Ardas, just before the wish for the good of all: chardi kala. Sikhs say them to one another as well, in easy times and hard ones. On an easy day they can sound like a slogan. But Sikhs remember decades when they were hunted and outnumbered, and in the stories of those camps, rising spirits had to mean something by nightfall. Today: chardi kala in the century.
screen: `TWO WORDS NEAR THE END OF THE ARDAS.` → `SAID IN EASY TIMES AND HARD.` → `TESTED BY NIGHTFALL IN THE CAMPS.`

segments.voice: Sikhs translate chardi kala as rising spirits, or ever-ascending spirit. It isn't cheerfulness. It's a spirit that stays turned upward when everything outside is turned down. Three things show what it meant in the hard century. First, the night prayer. Sikhs end the day with Kirtan Sohila, and its first hymn, by Guru Nanak, speaks of the house where the Creator's praises are sung and reflected on, and asks that the song of praise be sung there. That's in paraphrase. The riders had no house. Tradition says they sang it anyway, quietly, in camps without lamps, and the camp became the house. Second, the Ardas. The half-line before the good of all joins two things: Nanak's Name, and chardi kala. In the prayer, rising spirits come from the Name, not from mood. A rider didn't have to feel brave; he had to keep remembering. Third, the humor, the same camp speech the Nihangs still keep. Tradition says the camps joked about their own hardship, giving poor things grand names, laughing at hunger rather than letting it win. Joking about yourself while the world tries to erase you is its own kind of courage. A song at night, a Name to lean on, a joke at your own expense. None of it changed the danger. It changed how they carried it. Hunted for decades, they still sang.

segments.voice: Choose a line you know that lifts you: a hymn, a verse, a song from childhood, or, if you pray, Waheguru said slowly. Hum or say it under your breath, once, then again, quietly, the way it would sound in a camp with no lamps. If nothing in you rises, that's fine; they sang either way.
chardi kala, rising spirits that came from the Name, kept in the camps with a night prayer and a joke at their own expense. Today's word.

884.title: Women who kept the homes
884.hook: while men rode, women farmed, hid, fed and taught
884.howItsDone: Sikh women take the name Kaur at initiation and share the same standing in the sangat; at home, families teach children the daily prayers and Gurmukhi, and Sikh talks honor the women who kept households through the persecutions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala: rising spirits from the Name, a night prayer in camps with no lamps. Today, the people the riders came home to.

A knock at a farmhouse door after dark. Two riders, exhausted, horses blown. The man of the house is away with a band of his own. The woman who opens the door has children asleep inside and soldiers searching the district. She has seconds to decide. The stories of this century follow the riders. But every rider came from a home, and somebody kept it standing while he was gone. Today: women who kept the homes.
screen: `A KNOCK AFTER DARK.` → `SECONDS TO DECIDE.` → `EVERY RIDER CAME FROM A HOME.`

segments.voice: Tradition remembers a long list. They farmed: with the men riding, the fields still had to be plowed, watered, harvested, and the grain hidden from tax collectors and raiders. They hid people: riders sheltered in village houses, in grain stores, behind a wall of fodder, with a woman at the door answering questions calmly. They fed: the grain that reached the camps came from somebody's kitchen. And they taught. Tradition says that with gurdwaras watched or seized, the prayers and the Gurmukhi letters passed from mothers to children at home, by heart. That's one way a scripture survives persecution: at kitchen tables. Set that beside the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Nanak, in a passage Sikhs return to, asks why anyone would speak ill of woman, from whom kings are born. That's in paraphrase. He describes life itself as running through women: we're born of them, bound to them, and the world goes on through them. And Sikh tradition says the Khalsa gave women their own name, Kaur, alongside the men's Singh, with the same initiation and the same standing before the Guru. Not long ago you met the mothers in the governor's prison who kept faith. The women who kept the homes had a quieter courage, spread over years of answering the door. The chronicles followed the riders. But the riders had somewhere to come back to, because she held it together.

If you pray, let each breath out be a quiet Waheguru for her.

885.title: What the century teaches
885.hook: faith, courage and shared food carried a small people through
885.howItsDone: Sikhs teach Guru Nanak's way as naam japo, kirat karo and vand chhako, remembering the Name, honest work and sharing, and they tell the stories of the hard century as that way lived under pressure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kaur, and the women who farmed, hid, fed and taught while the riders were gone. She held it together. Today, what got them all through.

A saddlebag. Leather, worn soft, small enough to sling behind a rider. Open one from the hard century and what's inside? Some flour, maybe. A little salt. A wrapped bundle of prayers in Gurmukhi. In the stories, beside a horse and a weapon, that's close to everything a hunted rider owned. Yet the people who carried bags like that came through the century, still a people, still praying, still feeding strangers. So what got them through?
screen: `A WORN SADDLEBAG.` → `FLOUR, SALT, A BUNDLE OF PRAYERS.` → `WHAT GOT THEM THROUGH?`

segments.voice: Sikhs sum up Guru Nanak's teaching in three short phrases: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn honestly; vand chhako, share what you have. Hold them up against the hard century and you'll find them there, with courage standing beside them. First, the Name. The riders said the morning prayers from memory, opened the Granth wherever they stopped, and sang Kirtan Sohila in camps without lamps. The Ardas ties rising spirits to the Name. When everything else could be taken, the Name couldn't. Second, courage, but not the courage of revenge. The Ardas remembers the martyrs by what they endured and names no enemy. The courage the century hands on stands, shields the families, rebuilds at the ruins, and answers the door after dark. Third, honest bread, shared. Guru Nanak, in the Guru Granth Sahib, says in paraphrase that one who earns by work and gives some of it with their own hands has recognized the way. That's kirat and vand in one line. The Khalsa put the cooking pot before the sword, kept a common pot in the forests, and fed whoever came to the fire. So the saddlebag holds a Name, a backbone, a pot. None of them is heavy. All of them can be shared. None needed a building, a treasury or a government. And it doesn't take a war to apply. On an ordinary Tuesday, the question is the one the riders lived: what carries you?

886.title: The hard century close
886.hook: from Banda to Lahore: the hard century remembered in every Ardas
886.howItsDone: Sikhs say the Ardas standing at the close of prayers and gatherings, and its martyrs' passage remembers by their deeds the Sikhs of the persecutions; the congregation answers Waheguru after it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the saddlebag: the Name, courage without revenge, and vand chhako, sharing what you have. Today, the hard century comes to a close.

Weeks ago on this path, a Guru at Nanded met an ascetic who became Banda, the servant, and rode north with five arrows. Since then: towns taken and lost, a siege in a mud fort, a march to Delhi, a scholar executed for a festival, a humble nawab, forests and deserts, two holocausts, a temple blown up and rebuilt, Sirhind, and chiefs riding into Lahore. A long road. And all of it, Sikhs say, is folded into a few lines they say standing. Today: the hard century close.
screen: `FROM BANDA AND FIVE ARROWS.` → `SIEGES, FORESTS, TWO HOLOCAUSTS.` → `TO CHIEFS RIDING INTO LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Go back to the Ardas passage you met a few days ago. It remembers Sikhs cut limb from limb, scalped, broken on the wheel, who gave their heads but kept their faith, who kept their hair to the last breath, who gave their lives for the gurdwaras. The prayer doesn't name them. But Sikhs listening hear particular people. Tradition links cut limb from limb to Bhai Mani Singh, whom you met at the Diwali gathering. Broken on the wheel calls up the father and son, Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh. Scalped calls up Bhai Taru Singh, who, tradition says, gave up his scalp rather than his hair. So much of the century you just walked through is inside the prayer. Second, who says it. Not historians first. A grandmother at dawn. A child at a school assembly. A family before a long drive. A congregation after a wedding. The hard century is kept in the mouths of ordinary people, standing, hands folded. Third, the tone. The passage remembers what was endured, then the Ardas moves on to ask for the Name, for humility, for the good of all. Memory, then asking, then a wish for everyone. That's the shape these weeks have followed: the servant and his arrows, the hunted years, the ruins, the turn, and a people still singing at the end. All that story lives in a prayer said standing. Remembered in every Ardas.

887.title: What a misl was
887.hook: a misl was a band of equals with its own chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa
887.howItsDone: Sikhs learn about the misls in Sikh histories and at gurdwara talks, and the gurmata, a decision made together in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, is still part of how the Panth gathers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hard century's close: its martyrs remembered in every Ardas. Today, a new stretch of the story begins.

A rider comes into Amritsar with a few dozen horsemen behind him. Another arrives from the north with his own men, and another from across the river. None of them is king of the others. Each band has its own chief, its own villages, its own way of doing things. But when they reach the Guru's city, they sit down together as one Khalsa. For the next part of this path, those bands are the story, and the name for the band itself is today's word: misl.
screen: `RIDERS FROM EVERY DIRECTION.` → `EACH BAND WITH ITS OWN CHIEF.` → `ONE KHALSA AT AMRITSAR.`

segments.voice: Four turns. First, a misl was a band. Tradition says it gathered around a chief, a sardar, who had earned the trust of the riders with him. It held land and protected the villages under it, and those villages paid it for that protection. Second, a band of equals. In the way Sikh histories tell it, a rider wasn't the chief's servant. He was a Singh of the Khalsa who had chosen to ride with this sardar, and tradition says he could leave and ride with another. What was won was shared out. The chief led people who stood on the same ground he did. Third, the misls didn't stand alone. Together they made up the Dal Khalsa, the army of the Khalsa, and when a danger was too big for one band, they rode as one. Tradition says that at the great gatherings in Amritsar, the Sarbat Khalsa, the chiefs met before the Guru Granth Sahib and agreed on a gurmata, a resolution in the Guru's presence, which bound every band. Fourth, the misls were what the hard century produced. Small bands that had hidden in forests and deserts now held the countryside. Over the coming days, the path visits them one by one: who led them, where they rode, what each became. Some grew strong. Some stayed small. One would one day give rise to a kingdom. But they started in the same place: a band of equals.

888.title: The Bhangi misl
888.hook: the strongest early misl, holding Lahore and Amritsar for a time
888.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Bhangi misl in Sikh histories and in stories about Lahore and Amritsar, where the band's fort and the great gun are remembered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misl: a band around a chief, a band of equals, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa. Today, the first band by name.

A huge bronze cannon sits on a street in Lahore. Tradition says people in the Punjab once had a nickname for it, a name that had nothing to do with whoever cast it. They named it after the Sikh band that held it: the Bhangis' gun. A band that could keep hold of a gun like that, in a city like Lahore, was no small band. Today: the Bhangi misl.
screen: `A GREAT GUN IN LAHORE.` → `CALLED THE BHANGIS' GUN.` → `A BAND THAT HELD A CITY.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Tradition says it came from one of the band's early leaders, who was fond of bhang, a drink made from hemp, and the nickname stuck to the whole misl. Sikh histories tell it lightly, and the name outlived the habit: a nickname can outlast anyone remembering why. Second, reach. In the way Sikh histories tell it, the Bhangis grew fast after the hard century, and their chiefs held land across a wide stretch of the Punjab. In Amritsar, tradition says, they built a fort and held parts of the Guru's city. When the Dal Khalsa took Lahore, Bhangi chiefs were among those who shared and ruled it. The governor's city and the Guru's city, with one misl's riders in both. Third, the gun. Tradition says the Bhangis captured the great cannon, and it stayed with them long enough to carry their name, a sign of their strength. Fourth, the part in today's line. It didn't last. The later Bhangi chiefs were not the riders their fathers had been, as Sikh histories tell it, and they quarreled with each other. In time Lahore passed to another misl's leader, a young man you'll meet later on this path. Amritsar too. Strength gathered in one generation was spent in the next. The Bhangis were real, and they were strong. For a time.

889.title: The Ahluwalia misl
889.hook: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia's misl, later the state of Kapurthala
889.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Jassa Singh Ahluwalia in Sikh histories and gurdwara talks as a leader of the Dal Khalsa, and the Ahluwalia name lives on in families and in the town of Kapurthala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhangis, named for bhang, with their great gun and two cities, strong for a time. Today, a band known for one man.

Two hats. That was today's chief's problem. You've met Jassa Singh Ahluwalia on this path already: the boy who sang kirtan, the young rider Nawab Kapur Singh trained, the man the Khalsa called Sultan-ul-Qaum. Today, a different side. He had his own band, with its own riders and villages to look after. And he was the one the chiefs looked to when all the bands rode together. Lead your own people, and lead everyone. Today: the Ahluwalia misl.
screen: `TWO HATS.` → `HIS OWN BAND.` → `AND THE WHOLE DAL KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Four pieces. The name: tradition says Jassa Singh's family came from a village called Ahlu, near Lahore, and his band took its name from it, Ahluwalia, the ones from Ahlu. The first hat: as chief of his own misl, he had riders who had chosen to ride with him and villages that looked to his band for protection. That's a sardar's ordinary work: keep your people fed, safe and together. The second hat: tradition says that when the bands gathered at Amritsar and rode as the Dal Khalsa, the chiefs put Jassa Singh at the head. Think what that asks of a man. When spoils are shared, does his own band get the best? When there's a hard job, does it go to someone else's riders? In the way Sikh histories tell it, the other chiefs trusted him, and that trust is the whole point. A leader of everyone can't lead only for his own. Last, what the band became. Long after the riding years, the lands of the Ahluwalia misl became the state of Kapurthala, ruled by chiefs who carried the Ahluwalia name. The band outlasted the age of bands. Other misls are remembered for a fort, a flag, a river or a fight. This one is remembered for who led it, and because he was trusted beyond it. The leader's misl.

Notice whether they were fair to people who weren't their own, and what made you trust them. On each breath, be thankful for one thing they did, with Waheguru on the breath out if you pray.
